doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: First gig at twelve in a roadhouse trio
summary: A neighbor saxophonist takes him on a summer gig and teaches him accompaniment.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: But anyway, so for a while there, I guess almost to the time I learned bebop, I was a boogie woogie piano player. And not exclusively though, because I remember when I was about, oh about twelve years old I guess, we had moved to another place. My father took the piano with him too, he didn’t leave it there. And upstairs over us was a saxophone player, who had a gig on weekends. And his piano player got sick like just before the gig. And there was only three pieces, piano, drums and saxophone. Now he had to have something you know to fill in with the piano. So he didn’t know what to do. So he asked my father, he says, “Let me take Junior on the gig.” I guess he figured well as long as somebody’s there. It wasn’t a jazz club, it was like one of those they used to call it “road houses,” you know out on the highway, and nobody’s paying that much attention anyway. So I went and that night he taught me how to accompany the horns and everything. It was a style they call “moonshine,” you know like it as [scats] type of accompaniment. And he showed me the chords to play. Because most of the things he played were either blues chords or “I Got Rhythm.” In other words, the basic things all jazz musicians should learn to begin with. So I learned it there, and then I wound up keeping the gig all summer.
Wow. And you were how old?

Twelve. And when school opened again I couldn’t do it. But I learned a lot though. You know and then I learned other tunes too, like getting away from the “I Got Rhythm,” and the blues thing. And then along came bebop. Why did they ever teach me that? I haven’t been the same since — still trying to learn.
